title: Kernel Sandboxing, Bandwidth Controls, and Cooperative Shepherding Manual
author: Aisha Patel
content:
Overview:

This document defines the design, operational controls, and incident procedures for the Kernel Sandboxing and Cooperative Shepherding subsystem (KSCS). KSCS is the combination of: the sandbox controller that constrains per-cohort resource "bandwidth", an admission/governor layer that enforces soft and hard limits, and a cooperative shepherding protocol between the scheduler and kernel plugins to enable graceful handoff, preemption-friendly slices, and prioritized progress for latency‑sensitive requests.

Scope and intent:
- Scope: Applies to the runtime kernel and scheduler integrations used by Redwood’s hosted and dedicated inference clusters.
- Intent: Reduce noisy-neighbor and runaway kernel behavior while preserving tail latency for high-priority tiers and enabling safe experimental kernel rollouts.

Design goals:
1) Safety: prevent single tenant/cohort from starving others; avoid node OOMs and GPU hangs.
2) Latency preservation: keep high-priority request P99 within SLOs where possible.
3) Observability: expose deterministic telemetry for allocation and handoff decisions.
4) Replayability: allow deterministic replay of scheduling decisions for investigation.

Architecture overview:
- Components:
  - Sandbox Controller (sandboxd): central agent per node that negotiates quota windows, issues bandwidth tokens, and exposes an RPC for kernel plugin sync.
  - Kernel Plugin Interface (KPI): light-weight ABI inside each kernel that accepts token credits, preemption hints, and cooperative-shepherding callbacks.
  - Bandwidth Governor: admission service in the scheduler that translates request characteristics into bandwidth profiles (tokens/sec, max-slice-ms, priority).
  - Shepherd Agent: cross-node coordinator for multi-stage requests (e.g., multi-shard KV cache warmups) that requests temporary credits and releases them on completion.

How it works (high level):
1) Request classified by admission -> bandwidth profile assigned (e.g., interactive-high, batch-background).
2) Scheduler requests token allocation from sandboxd for the chosen cohort. sandboxd enforces cohort global windows using a leaky-bucket model.
3) Kernel receives tokens and can run a slice up to configured max-slice-ms. If a higher priority request arrives, kernel uses cooperative callback to yield at a safe boundary.
4) Shepherd Agent mediates long-running handoffs (for example, model swap or large KV prefetch) to avoid long blocking of interactive slots.

Terminology:
- token: smallest unit of bandwidth credit (represents a short amount of GPU work permissable).
- cohort: a classification of traffic (customer-tier + workload-class).
- slice: contiguous execution window inside a kernel invocation (bounded by max-slice-ms).
- shepherding: cooperative handoff process where a running kernel segment coordinates with scheduler to release or re-acquire credits gracefully.

Modeled policies and examples:
- Leaky-bucket parameters (default):
  - bucket_size_tokens: 10_000
  - refill_rate_tokens_per_sec: 5_000
  - max_burst_tokens: 15_000
- Priority mapping (example):
  - interactive-high: tokens/sec 5_000, max-slice-ms 6, preemption-grace-ms 2
  - interactive-low: tokens/sec 2_000, max-slice-ms 8, preemption-grace-ms 4
  - batch-background: tokens/sec 1_000, max-slice-ms 50, preemption-grace-ms 20

Config table (YAML sample for sandboxd per-node):

node_id: node-az1-gpu-123
sandboxd:
  bucket_size_tokens: 10000
  refill_rate_tokens_per_sec: 5000
  max_burst_tokens: 15000
  cohort_defaults:
    interactive-high:
      tokens_per_sec: 5000
      max_slice_ms: 6
      preemption_grace_ms: 2
    interactive-low:
      tokens_per_sec: 2000
      max_slice_ms: 8
      preemption_grace_ms: 4
    batch-background:
      tokens_per_sec: 1000
      max_slice_ms: 50
      preemption_grace_ms: 20

Important telemetry and metrics (exposed via /metrics and traces):
- sandboxd_cohort_tokens_total{cohort, node} (counter)
- sandboxd_cohort_tokens_available{cohort, node} (gauge)
- kernel_slice_duration_ms{cohort, kernel_variant} (histogram)
- shepherd_handoff_success_total (counter)
- preemption_yield_count{cohort} (counter)
- kernel_blocked_on_tokens{node} (gauge)
- p99_latency_by_cohort{cohort} (derived)

Alerting thresholds (recommended):
- sandboxd_cohort_tokens_available drops below 10% for more than 30s for interactive-high -> P1 oncall paging.
- kernel_blocked_on_tokens spikes > 3 nodes in 1m -> P0 investigation (potential global throttling).
- shepherd_handoff_success_total failure rate > 2% over 10m -> P2 ticket.

Scheduling hooks and API (summary):
- RequestClassification(request) -> cohort, profile_id
- SandboxRequestTokens(profile_id, amount) -> granted_tokens, lease_ms
- KernelYieldHint(current_slice_ms, grace_ms) -> ok_to_yield
- ShepherdAcquire(resource_id, expected_duration_ms) -> temporary_credit_handle
- ShepherdRelease(handle) -> release_ack

Rollout checklist for kernel-side changes (safe deployment):
1) Create a feature flag for KPI changes and ensure sandboxd reads dynamic config.
2) Run unit tests and KPI ABI checks in kernel-sandbox CI.
3) Canary deploy with 0.5% traffic, monitor kernel_slice_duration_ms and preemption_yield_count.
4) If p99 latency regression > 8% or shepherd_handoff failures > 1% in 30m, rollback.
5) Gradually increase traffic in doubling steps (0.5%, 1%, 2%, 4%, 8%, 16%) with 30m steady windows.

Incident triage runbook (fast path):
1) Symptoms: high P99 for interactive-high with kernel_blocked_on_tokens > 0 and tokens_available < 5%.
2) Run: kubectl exec to sandboxd on affected node(s) and run admin /debug/token-state.
3) If a single cohort is consuming > 80% of tokens, identify the tenant and either:
   a) Apply temporary cohort-hold via admission to reduce tokens/sec by 50%, or
   b) Evict long-running background batch pods from the node.
4) If multiple nodes show kernel_blocked_on_tokens, trigger global mitigation: scale dedicated GPU pool up by +20% and enable degraded-routing policy to fallback model-variant with lower memory.
5) Create an incident page, attach sandboxd token dumps, kernel traces, and shepherd agent logs.

Experiment & benchmark protocol (how to measure effects):
1) Goal: validate that KSCS reduces cross-cohort interference while maintaining P99 SLO for interactive-high.
2) Synthetic corpus: mix of short interactive requests (median tokens 40, 90% < 120 tokens) and long prefetchs (median 2k tokens).
3) Bench steps:
   a) Baseline: run workload on current kernel w/o KSCS active for 1 hour. Capture p50/p95/p99 and per-cohort token consumption.
   b) Activation: enable KSCS sandboxd with conservative refill rates and run for 1 hour.
   c) Stress: drive a background cohort to 300% of normal rate and measure regressions.
4) Success criteria:
   - interactive-high p99 delta <= +5% compared to baseline under normal load.
   - Under stress, interactive-high p99 should degrade less than baseline (target < +30% delta).
   - shepherd_handoff_success_total >= 99.5%.

Testing checklist (local/dev):
- Unit tests for KPI ABI compatibility.
- Local sandboxd simulator with configurable leak rates.
- Synthetic trace replay harness (see related pages) to reproduce burst shapes.

Operational notes and ownership:
- Owners: Runtime Scheduling Team (primary), Runtime Observability (secondary).
- Slack channels: #runtime-schedule, #runtime-ops. Use the incident template when paging.

Known limitations and caveats:
- Some third-party kernel plugins may not implement cooperative yield hooks; we provide a compatibility shim that converts hard preemption to softer slice truncation but may increase tail variance.
- Token accounting introduces small overhead (~1–2% CPU per sandboxd node) and additional trace volume; budget observability accordingly.
- KSCS reduces but does not eliminate cross-node emergent backpressure when NVLink or PCIe saturation occurs; use combined network+sandboxd alarms in those cases.

Appendix A — Troubleshooting commands:
- sandboxd debug token summary:
  curl -sS http://sandboxd.local/debug/token-state | jq .
- show recent yields and preemptions from kernel traces:
  <internal-trace-query> | filter event:kpi_yield | sort -desc timestamp | limit 200

Appendix B — Short FAQ:
Q: What happens if shepherding fails mid-handoff?
A: The shepherd agent rolls back the temporary credit and marks the resource as "quarantined" for 60s; background cohorts are deprioritized and telemetry recorded for follow-up.

Q: Can we bypass KSCS for emergencies?
A: Yes — emergency flagging route exists but requires sign-off from SRE/Runtime leads and leaves an audit trail; misuse will trigger automatic review.
